name: Mitochondrial Complex IV Deficiency (Cytochrome c Oxidase Deficiency)

clinicalPearls: Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase, COX) is the terminal enzyme of the electron transport chain, transferring electrons from cytochrome c to molecular oxygen using haem a/a3 and copper centres while pumping protons.

Isolated COX deficiency is one of the commonest respiratory chain defects in childhood and a frequent biochemical cause of Leigh syndrome; most cases are due to nuclear assembly-factor defects rather than the mtDNA-encoded catalytic subunits MT-CO1, MT-CO2 and MT-CO3.
SURF1 is the prototypical nuclear cause of COX-deficient Leigh syndrome, producing symmetrical brainstem and basal ganglia lesions, hypertrichosis and progressive neurological regression.

SCO2 and COX15 defects cause a fatal infantile hypertrophic cardioencephalomyopathy, and SCO1 and COX10 cause hepatopathic or tubulopathic (renal Fanconi) presentations, reflecting the copper-handling and haem a-synthesis roles of these factors.
LRPPRC variants cause the Leigh syndrome French-Canadian (Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean) type, with a distinctive tendency to lethal, acidotic and hyperlactataemic metabolic crises and facial dysmorphism.
Histochemistry classically shows COX-negative fibres, and ragged-red or COX-deficient fibres support a mitochondrial myopathy; enzymology confirms isolated reduction of Complex IV activity.
TACO1 (a translational activator of COX1) gives a later-onset Leigh-like syndrome, illustrating that defects of mtDNA translation specific to COX subunits also present as isolated COX deficiency.

Benign infantile mitochondrial myopathy with a reversible COX deficiency (associated with a homoplasmic MT-TE variant) can recover spontaneously, so a poor prognosis should not be assumed prematurely.
reference.pathophysiology: Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) is the final electron acceptor of the respiratory chain, receiving electrons from reduced cytochrome c and using them to reduce molecular oxygen to water at a binuclear haem a3-copperB centre, while translocating protons to sustain the membrane potential that drives ATP synthase. Its three catalytic core subunits (COX1, COX2 and COX3) are encoded by mitochondrial DNA (MT-CO1, MT-CO2, MT-CO3) and carry the haem and copper redox centres, whereas the numerous supernumerary subunits and, critically, a large network of nuclear-encoded assembly and metallation factors are required to build the mature enzyme. Autosomal recessive variants in these nuclear factors are the predominant cause: SURF1 (a general assembly factor), SCO1 and SCO2 (mitochondrial copper delivery), COX10 and COX15 (haem a biosynthesis), COX6B1, PET100, the translational activator TACO1, and LRPPRC (which stabilises and polyadenylates mitochondrial mRNAs); maternally inherited MT-CO variants also occur. Loss of terminal oxidase activity halts electron flow to oxygen, collapses proton-motive force and oxidative phosphorylation, and generates lactic acidosis, with tissue-specific damage in brain (Leigh syndrome), heart (SCO2/COX15 cardiomyopathy), liver and renal tubule reflecting the differing roles of each assembly factor.
additionalDifferentials: Mitochondrial Complex I deficiency (NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase defect)
Mitochondrial Complex III deficiency (cytochrome bc1 / BCS1L defect)
Mitochondrial Complex V deficiency (ATP synthase defect)
Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex deficiency and biotinidase deficiency (other treatable Leigh-like disorders)
Combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiencies from mtDNA depletion and translation defects
Other causes of infantile hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (Pompe disease, other mitochondrial and metabolic cardiomyopathies)
Fatal and benign infantile mitochondrial myopathy (reversible COX deficiency associated with the MT-TE variant)
additionalInvestigations: Blood and cerebrospinal fluid lactate and pyruvate with lactate-to-pyruvate ratio
Urine organic acids and renal tubular function screen for Fanconi syndrome
Muscle histochemistry for COX-negative fibres and ragged-red fibres, with combined COX/SDH staining
Spectrophotometric respiratory chain enzymology showing isolated Complex IV deficiency
Neuroimaging for symmetrical basal ganglia and brainstem lesions typical of Leigh syndrome
Molecular testing of nuclear genes (SURF1, SCO1, SCO2, COX10, COX15, COX6B1, LRPPRC, TACO1, PET100) and MT-CO genes
Echocardiography for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and liver function tests where hepatopathy is suspected
redFlags: Progressive brainstem dysfunction with abnormal breathing, apnoea or bulbar failure in Leigh syndrome
Fatal infantile hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with heart failure (SCO2/COX15 phenotype)
Severe lactic acidotic crises in the French-Canadian LRPPRC phenotype, often triggered by illness or fever
Hepatic failure or refractory metabolic acidosis in the neonatal period
Rapid neurological regression with loss of acquired milestones
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is generally poor for SURF1-related Leigh syndrome, the SCO2/COX15 cardioencephalomyopathies and LRPPRC French-Canadian disease, which are frequently fatal in infancy or early childhood; however, the reversible infantile COX-deficient myopathy can recover, and milder later-onset forms follow a more protracted course.
pitfalls: Assuming all infantile COX deficiency is fatal and missing the reversible MT-TE-associated benign infantile myopathy.
Failing to recognise the French-Canadian LRPPRC phenotype and its propensity for sudden lethal acidotic crises.
Overlooking treatable mimics such as biotinidase deficiency and pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency before concluding COX deficiency.
Interpreting patchy COX-negative fibres as normal when only a proportion of fibres are affected.
Not screening the heart and renal tubule, missing the cardiomyopathic and Fanconi phenotypes tied to specific assembly-factor genes.
